title: Modern Applications of Laser Spectroscopy
lead: A short survey of how researchers put laser light to work on atoms and molecules: single wavelengths that pick out one species or one energy change, short pulses that follow processes in time, and intensities high enough to make a plasma or drive nonlinear effects.
notes: Written by Stephanie Schaertel (Grand Valley State University), with references edited by Tom Neils (Grand Rapids Community College), shared under CC BY-NC-SA 4.0.
exercise_notes: The section prints no exercises; the one here is new and AI-written, with its Bloom level and concept tags chosen by AI.

exercises.source_id: Overall, lasers are especially useful as light sources when one or more of the following properties are desired
exercises.prompt: A chemist wants to follow how an excited molecule falls apart over the first few picoseconds after it absorbs light. Which property of laser light does the experiment rely on most?

answer.hint: The question is about when things happen.
answer.solution: Following a process over picoseconds is a time-resolved study: one short pulse starts the process and later pulses probe it, so the pulses must be shorter than the times being measured. Monochromaticity would pick out a species or an energy change, and tight focus or coherence would matter for where the light goes, but none of them gives the timing.
